name: Brandenburg Gate
label: Brandenburg Gate
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Pariser Platz' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Pariser Platz' (way/38210407): middle (193 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/206159289: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline '' (21 m across).
notes: Berlin's best-known landmark, on Pariser Platz.

text.description:
The Brandenburg Gate is one of Berlin's best-known landmarks, a neoclassical monument built between 1788 and 1791 for King Frederick William II of Prussia. The architect was Carl Gotthard Langhans. Twelve fluted Doric columns, six along each side, form five passageways. Above them stands the Quadriga, a bronze chariot drawn by four horses and driven by a goddess figure, made by the sculptor Johann Gottfried Schadow. Through the Cold War the Berlin Wall blocked the gateway, and since 1990 the gate has stood as a symbol of unity and peace.

It photographs well because it is symmetrical and the stone is pale. The cobbled square in front gives your frame some depth. The classic view is the full-frontal one from Pariser Platz, where the six columns and the Quadriga sit centred and the horses face towards you. Stand on the east side of the square and look west.

The square gets very crowded from late morning, so arrive early if you want an empty foreground. Keep your phone level and use the gridlines so the columns stay upright. If people wander into the frame, take several shots and pick the cleanest. For a different angle, the western side, along Straße des 17. Juni, shows the gate in late-day light with the Quadriga seen from behind.
text.geographic_location: The gate is in the western part of Berlin's city centre, in the district of Mitte. It stands where Unter den Linden meets Ebertstraße, with the Reichstag building one block to the north and the Tiergarten park to the west.
text.directions_text: No nearby Underground, S-Bahn or tram stops are listed for this spot. The gate is on Pariser Platz, at the end of Unter den Linden. If you are walking along Unter den Linden from the direction of Berlin Cathedral, keep heading west and the gate is at the end of the avenue. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x), which fits the whole gate with the square in front of it. Switch to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the Quadriga and the column details. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of cobbles and sky, and keep the gate in the middle of the frame so the edges do not stretch.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Pariser Platz (east side of the square, facing west toward the gate). The gate's front with the six columns and the Quadriga centred above, with the cobbled square in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the centre of the gate up with the middle vertical line, with the Quadriga on top. Hold the phone level so the columns do not lean. Include a strip of cobbles at the bottom for depth. For an alternative, try an angled view from the edge of Pariser Platz with the surrounding buildings partly in the frame, or walk round to Straße des 17. Juni for the western face.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the gate to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the stone keeps its detail. Take a few shots in a row so you can choose one without people in the way. Night mode can help after dark, but the floodlighting is switched off from 26 October to early December 2026 for renewal, so night shots may not work then.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise is best, when the square is quiet and the sun is behind you. Late morning onwards is very crowded. The Festival of Lights and New Year's Eve bring large crowds and possible restrictions, so check current conditions before you go.

text.access_note: The gate stands in an open public square, but check the official site before you go for events, closures or restrictions.

name: Reichstag building
label: Reichstag
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Platz der Republik' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Platz der Republik' (way/499593498): middle (321 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/2201742: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Reichstag Building' (172 m across).
notes: Seat of the German parliament with its glass dome.

text.description: The Reichstag is the seat of Germany's Bundestag, and the lawn in front of it gives the classic straight-on view. The building went up between 1884 and 1894 to designs by Paul Wallot. After wartime damage and decades of partial use, it was redesigned by Norman Foster between 1995 and 1999 and handed over for parliament use in April 1999. The walk-in glass dome is the best-known part of that rebuild. Look above the main entrance for the words "Dem deutschen Volke", added in 1916. The old stone and the modern glass in one frame are what make the view work. The wide lawn keeps the foreground clear, so you can step back until the whole façade fits. The lawn was reported muddy and under groundworks in June 2025, so check its condition on the day. For a second angle, the Marie-Elisabeth-Lüders-Haus, across the Spree, shows the Reichstag and dome with the river reflecting the buildings. Only the lower public level of the double bridge there is open to visitors. The dome and rooftop terrace give close-up views of the glass and the spiral ramp, but they need advance online registration.
text.geographic_location: The Reichstag stands in the Tiergarten district, on the left bank of the River Spree, on Platz der Republik.
text.directions_text: The U-Bahn station Bundestag is the stop named for reaching the lawn in front of the west façade, and from there you head for Platz der Republik. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the whole west front with the dome behind. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are close or the building will not fit. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the dome or the inscription above the entrance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Platz der Republik (open lawn directly in front of the west façade). The full west front of the Reichstag with its columns and the glass dome rising behind, framed by open grass. The Reichstag lies to the east of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the entrance on the centre line so the columns look straight. Keep a band of lawn at the bottom to frame the building and leave the dome clear above it. For a different view, the Marie-Elisabeth-Lüders-Haus across the Spree shows the Reichstag and dome with the river reflecting the buildings.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky stays blue and the stone keeps its detail. Hold the phone level, using the gridlines, to avoid leaning verticals.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Afternoon, when the sun is behind you as you face the building, according to one traveller review. Go early if you want fewer people in the frame.

text.access_note: The lawn on Platz der Republik is open public space, but check its condition first; the dome and rooftop terrace need advance online registration, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The default lens (1x) should be wide enough to fit the full west front from the lawn; the ultra-wide (0.5x) helps if you stand closer.
The Bundestag U-Bahn station is the nearest stop to the lawn.
The west façade faces west, so an afternoon sun is behind a photographer looking east towards it.
Early in the day there are usually fewer people in the frame.

name: Checkpoint Charlie
label: Checkpoint Charlie
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Checkpoint Charlie' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/417346627: the OpenStreetMap point 'Checkpoint Charlie'.
notes: Former Cold War border crossing.

text.description:
Checkpoint Charlie was the best-known crossing point between East and West Berlin during the Cold War. Today the junction of Friedrichstraße and Zimmerstraße is a busy city crossroads, but a replica guardhouse stands in the middle of the street, with its 'You are leaving the American Sector' sign, sandbags and flags. It is one of the most photographed spots in Berlin, and it is easy to see why: the booth, the sign and the street around it tell the story in a single frame.

A few facts help you read the scene. The name comes from the letter C in the NATO phonetic alphabet. In October 1961, ten Soviet and ten American tanks stood facing each other near here, and the stand-off ended peacefully on 28 October. The guardhouse you see now is a replica; the metal container that replaced the original wooden shed in 1976 is on display at the Allied Museum in Dahlem, not here.

For your phone, the main job is to get the booth and sign clear of people and traffic. Expect crowds, and take care at the junction, as cars keep moving past. Photograph from the pavement and never step into the road to get a better angle. Costumed actors sometimes pose with visitors, and photos with them may cost a few euros, so ask first if you want a picture with them. Nearby, the outdoor history panels of the Checkpoint Charlie Gallery make a good second picture, with escape stories in the foreground and the street behind.
text.geographic_location: Checkpoint Charlie is in the Friedrichstadt district of central Berlin, at the junction of Friedrichstraße and Zimmerstraße, close to Mauerstraße.
text.directions_text: No nearby station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from the Friedrichstadt area of central Berlin, around Friedrichstraße, and follow Friedrichstraße to the junction with Zimmerstraße. If you are coming from further away, go by taxi. The phone icon on the map is at the replica booth itself, so you can walk straight up to it. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the booth, sign and street in one frame. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the pavement is crowded and you cannot step back, but keep the booth away from the edges, where it can look stretched. A touch of zoom (2x) helps you pick out the sign and flags from the kerb.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here you see the guardhouse with its 'You are leaving the American Sector' sign, sandbags and flags, framed by the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the booth on one of the vertical lines so the sign stays readable. Keep the phone level so the street edges do not lean. Wait for a gap in the people, or let a few figures in as a sense of scale. For a second picture, try the Checkpoint Charlie Gallery panels nearby, with the checkpoint area behind them.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the sign to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the flags keep their colour. Take a few shots in a row, as people and cars move through the frame all the time.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when crowds and traffic are lighter.

text.access_note: This is an open public street junction, but traffic is busy, so stay on the pavement and check the official site before you go if you plan to visit any nearby exhibition.

name: Berlin Wall Memorial
label: Berlin Wall Memorial
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Dokumentationszentrum Berliner Mauer' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Gedenkstätte Berliner Mauer (Dokumentationszentrum)' (way/45664094): middle (52 m across); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/14375945: large area 'Berlin Wall Memorial' (1388 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Preserved section of the border strip on Bernauer Straße.

text.description:
The Berlin Wall Memorial is a long stretch of Bernauer Straße where the border that divided the city is still readable on the ground. It was created in 1998 and commemorates the division of Berlin and the people who died at the Wall. It includes a 60-metre section of the border kept as it was when the Wall fell, a Chapel of Reconciliation, a visitor centre and the Documentation Centre. The preserved section is closed off, so you look at it from outside rather than walk through it.

From up there you look straight down on the preserved border strip. Both wall lines, the patrol road and a watchtower fit into one picture, and the TV Tower sits on the skyline. Seen from above, the layout makes sense in a way it doesn't at street level.

If you want a second set of shots, go down to the street. The reconstructed wall, the watchtower and the rusted steel rods that trace the Wall's course look striking against the modern buildings behind them. The rods are easy to use as leading lines.

The Chapel of Reconciliation is also worth a frame. It is oval, with a façade of wooden rods, and it replaced a church that was destroyed in 1985 because it stood inside the border strip. Allow time for both the tower and the street, and keep your phone steady, for example by bracing your elbows, rather than holding it out at arm's length.
text.geographic_location: On Bernauer Straße in Mitte, Berlin, at the corner of Ackerstraße. The outdoor part of the memorial lies west of Berlin Nordbahnhof, and the visitor centre is at the corner of Gartenstraße.
text.directions_text: Head for Bernauer Straße in Mitte, and check public transport locally. The Documentation Centre, with its viewing tower, is on the opposite side of the street from the preserved wall section. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole strip. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the watchtower or the TV Tower, and use ultra-wide (0.5x) only for close shots at street level.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Dokumentationszentrum Berliner Mauer (rooftop viewing tower at Bernauer Straße 111, opposite the preserved death strip). A straight-down view of the preserved death strip, with both wall lines, the patrol road, a watchtower and the TV Tower on the skyline. The main memorial point lies just to the south.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the patrol road with one of the grid lines, so the two wall lines run cleanly through the frame. Keep the TV Tower on the skyline as a marker of place. For an alternative, go down to the Gedenkstätte Berliner Mauer grounds and shoot the reconstructed wall, the watchtower and the steel rods against the modern buildings.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the strip to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright so the detail on the ground is not washed out. Wipe the lens before you start.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft, even light, such as a bright overcast day, suits the view down onto the strip.

text.access_note: The outdoor grounds are open daily, but the viewing tower is inside the Documentation Centre and has set opening days, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Soft, even light such as a bright overcast day suits the view down onto the strip.
Dragging the exposure slider down a little helps when the sky is bright.

name: Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe
label: Holocaust Memorial
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Ebertstraße / Behrenstraße' (2 web pages); placed at crossing of Ebertstraße and Behrenstraße (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/172234733: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe' (240 m across).
notes: Field of concrete stelae near the Brandenburg Gate.

text.description: This memorial to the Jewish victims of the Holocaust was designed by architect Peter Eisenman with Buro Happold. It is a sloping field of 2,711 grey concrete slabs, called stelae, set out in a grid across 1.9 hectares. Each slab is the same length and width, but the heights run from 0.2 metres to 4.7 metres. The ground dips as you walk in, so the rows seem to rise around you. Building was finished in December 2004, and the memorial opened to the public in May 2005. It photographs well because the repeating lines give a phone camera plenty of perspective to work with. This northwest corner is an informal photo spot where visitors and tour groups gather to take pictures. Keep your shots calm and respectful. Climbing on the stelae is discouraged and staff will ask you to get down. For a wider view of the southern end with Potsdamer Platz behind it, try Ebertstraße. Once you are inside, narrow-alley shots and close-ups of the concrete work nicely too.
text.geographic_location: In the Mitte district of Berlin, one block south of the Brandenburg Gate, on the eastern edge of the Tiergarten. The address is Cora-Berliner-Straße 1.
text.directions_text: Start from the Brandenburg Gate and walk one block south. From there, the middle of the memorial is about 2 minutes on foot to the south-east. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole edge of the field and the rows running away. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a single row of slabs.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Ebertstraße and Behrenstraße (northwest corner of the memorial). The grey stelae field stretching away from the street corner, with the memorial's edge in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line the edge of the nearest slabs up with them, so the rows look straight. Crouch a little for a lower viewpoint that makes the slabs look taller. For a different view, walk to Ebertstraße and shoot along the southern end with Potsdamer Platz behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a mid-grey slab to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky is bright, so the concrete keeps its detail. Telephoto shots work best with your elbows tucked in and the phone held steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is usually the quietest, with fewer tour groups and school classes at the corner.

text.access_note: The open-air field is a public space that can be entered free at any hour; for the underground information centre, check the official site before you go.

sources.title: Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe

name: Alexanderplatz
label: Alexanderplatz
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Alexanderplatz' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Alexanderplatz' (way/783052052): middle (563 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/783052052: 'Fountain of the Peoples' Friendship', the best-known feature inside 'Alexanderplatz' (564 m across).
notes: Busy square with the World Clock.

text.description:
Alexanderplatz is a large public square and transport hub in Berlin's central Mitte district, and it is often the first place visitors head for. It photographs well because the TV Tower (Fernsehturm) rises right above the open space. The World Clock (Weltzeituhr) makes a ready-made foreground that tells people at once where you are and gives the tower a sense of scale. The Fountain of the Peoples' Friendship is the best-known feature on the square itself, so it makes a handy second subject.

The square is named after the Russian Tsar Alexander I, who was welcomed here on a parade ground in October 1805. King Frederick William III renamed the square on 2 November 1805. Before that it lay just outside the city wall by the George Gate, and it was a cattle market and later a major wool market. Today it is ringed by shops and department stores and is reputedly the most visited area of Berlin, so expect people in your frame.

For a phone photo, stand near the World Clock and look across the square toward the tower. Turn the phone upright to catch the full height of the tower, with the clock low in the frame. If you want a different angle, the steps at the Rotes Rathaus look back over the square from a little higher. The open ground at the Marx-Engels-Forum gives room for a wide view of the tower rising behind.
text.geographic_location: Alexanderplatz is in the central Mitte district of Berlin, close to the TV Tower (Fernsehturm) and a short distance from the Rotes Rathaus (Red City Hall).
text.directions_text: Head for Alexanderplatz itself in central Mitte. From there the fountain is about 1 minute on foot to the west. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the TV Tower with the World Clock in front of it. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole square and the tower in one frame. A telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) is useful for picking out the top of the tower or details of the fountain.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Alexanderplatz (near the World Clock (Weltzeituhr), looking across the square toward the tower). The TV Tower rising above the square, with the World Clock in the foreground to give scale and a clear sense of place. The Fountain of the Peoples' Friendship lies to the west of you if you want a second shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn the phone upright and switch on the gridlines. Put the World Clock on a lower third line and let the tower rise through the upper part of the frame. For a different view, the steps at the Rotes Rathaus show the tower from a higher angle with the square spread out below. The Marx-Engels-Forum has open ground for a wide shot with the tower behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the base of the tower to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the tower keeps its detail. Take a few frames, as people will keep walking through the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or later in the evening is likely to be quieter, but check the weather, because a clear sky helps the tower stand out.

text.access_note: Alexanderplatz is an open public square; for anything ticketed nearby, such as the TV Tower itself, check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The fountain lies to the west of the stand-here point, in line with the square's layout shown on the map.
Early morning or later in the evening is likely to be quieter on the square than the middle of the day.
A clear sky helps the TV Tower stand out against the background.
Alexanderplatz can be photographed from freely, as it is an open public space.
The steps at the Rotes Rathaus are a little higher than the square and look back over it.

name: East Side Gallery
label: East Side Gallery
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Mühlenstraße' (2 web pages); placed at crossing of Mühlenstraße and Warschauer Straße (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/6807791: large area 'East Side Gallery' (1001 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Longest surviving stretch of the Berlin Wall, covered in murals.

text.description:
The East Side Gallery is a long open-air gallery of murals painted straight onto a surviving stretch of the Berlin Wall, running along Mühlenstraße beside the Spree. The wall is 1,316 metres long. In spring 1990, soon after the Wall opened, 118 artists from 21 countries painted it, commenting on the political changes of 1989 and 1990. It is now a protected heritage monument.

It photographs well because the colour is everywhere and the wall gives you a long, simple line to work with. From there the painted wall fills the foreground and the towers of the Oberbaum Bridge rise behind it, so one frame holds both the Wall and the bridge.

For a close-up, walk a short way along the wall and fill the frame with a single mural. The famous 'Fraternal Kiss' painting by Dmitri Vrubel, showing Brezhnev and Honecker, is the obvious one to look for. Exactly where it sits along the wall is worth checking on the day. Some murals are sometimes covered during restoration work, and weekend crowds can block the main shots, so allow a little patience and take a few frames as people move through.
text.geographic_location: In Friedrichshain, on the Mühlenstraße side of the Spree, between Berlin Ostbahnhof and the Oberbaumbrücke. The Kreuzberg bank of the river is just across the water.
text.directions_text: Head for the Oberbaumbrücke end of Mühlenstraße. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the painted wall and the bridge towers into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view of a few murals together. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of a single painting.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Mühlenstraße and Warschauer Straße (the corner where the gallery begins, at the bridge end). The painted wall in the foreground with the Oberbaum Bridge towers rising behind it. The rest of the gallery stretches away to the west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the top of the wall up with a grid line so it does not tilt. Keep the wall running diagonally through the frame, with the bridge towers behind it. If you want a wide view along the Spree over the wall, with the bridge and the TV Tower in the distance, the Oberbaumbrücke is a second viewpoint. For the 'Fraternal Kiss' mural, move in close and fill the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the wall to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the paint does not look washed out. Hold the phone steady and take a few shots, as passers-by often walk through the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go on a weekday if you can, as weekend crowds can block the main shots.

text.access_note: The gallery is an open-air monument with no paid entry, but some murals can be covered during restoration work, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The ultra-wide lens is the easiest way to fit the wall and the bridge towers into one frame from the corner.

name: Berlin Cathedral
label: Berlin Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Lustgarten' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Lustgarten' (way/16000014): middle (272 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/313670734: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Berlin Cathedral' (140 m across).
notes: Domed Protestant church on Museum Island.

text.description:
Berlin Cathedral is the big green-domed church on the edge of the Lustgarten, on Museum Island in central Berlin. The building you see today went up between 1894 and 1905 for Emperor William II, to plans by Julius Raschdorff, in a Renaissance and Baroque Revival style. It is the largest Protestant church in Germany and also a major burial place of the Hohenzollern family. It was damaged in the Second World War, and the interior was restored by 2002.

It photographs well because the facade and dome are so symmetrical. From the Lustgarten you can face the cathedral head-on. Even on a phone, the open lawn and the paving in front give you natural leading lines that draw the eye up to the dome. The Lustgarten is a park, so it is free to reach on foot. It does get crowded through the day, so be patient and wait for a gap, or include a few people to give a sense of scale. A fountain and stone slabs in the foreground are seasonal, so what you see may differ from older photos.

If you want a different angle, the Karl-Liebknecht-Brücke shows the dome beside the Humboldt Forum facade and often the TV Tower. The Friedrichsbrücke gives a calmer view across the Spree, with fewer people in the frame.
text.geographic_location: The cathedral is in central Berlin, on Museum Island, on the edge of the Lustgarten park. The Spree runs close by.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so the easiest way in is to head for Museum Island in central Berlin and walk to the Lustgarten. The cathedral is to the north-east of it, about 2 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole facade and dome in from the Lustgarten, with plenty of lawn or paving in the foreground. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look with less stretching at the edges. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the dome and stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Lustgarten (front of the cathedral, facing the dome head-on). A symmetrical, head-on view of the green dome and facade, with the lawn and fountain or stone slabs as leading lines in the foreground. From here you face the dome head-on, with the cathedral to the north-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the centre of the dome with the middle vertical line so the symmetry looks deliberate. Keep your phone level, because tilting it up makes the building lean backwards. Use the paving or lawn edges as leading lines. For a different angle, try the Karl-Liebknecht-Brücke for the dome beside the Humboldt Forum, or the Friedrichsbrücke for a calmer view across the river.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the dome to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little. This stops the bright sky washing out the detail in the green copper dome. Wipe your lens first, as phone lenses pick up fingerprints easily.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: The Lustgarten is busy through the day, so early morning or later in the evening is likely to give you a clearer view. Check how the light looks on the facade when you arrive and adjust your exposure.

text.access_note: The Lustgarten is an open public park, but entry to the cathedral itself and any dome visits may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.

name: Potsdamer Platz
label: Potsdamer Platz
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Potsdamer Platz' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Potsdamer Platz' (relation/3200536): middle (225 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/3200536: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Potsdamer Platz' (226 m across).
notes: Modern square with skyscrapers.

text.description:
Potsdamer Platz is a public square and busy traffic intersection in the centre of Berlin. It takes its name from Potsdam, about 25 km to the south west. It marks the place where the old road from Potsdam passed through Berlin's city wall at the Potsdam Gate. In the 19th and early 20th centuries it grew into one of the busiest junctions in Europe. It was destroyed in the Second World War, and the Berlin Wall later ran straight through the area. The glass-and-steel buildings you see today mostly date from the redevelopment after 1990.

For photographs, the best-known subject is the Sony Center, with its distinctive roof, set against the glass towers around it. It is especially striking after dark, when the lit-up buildings suit a phone's night mode. Stand in front of the Sony Center and look up and across the square. You can include the roof, the towers and some of the street life below. By day, the mix of old-city history and modern architecture makes a good contrast shot. If you want a wider view, the Panoramapunkt gives a 360-degree outlook from about 100 m up. The Reichstag also shows the square from a distance, and a phone's telephoto lens can pick out the Sony Center from there.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Berlin, about 1 km south of the Brandenburg Gate and the Reichstag, close to the south-east corner of the Tiergarten park.
text.directions_text: From the Brandenburg Gate or the Reichstag, head south for about 1 km to reach Potsdamer Platz. Once on the square, look for the Sony Center and stand in front of it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the Sony Center roof and the surrounding towers into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view of the buildings. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the roof or the tops of the towers.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Potsdamer Platz (in front of the Sony Center). The square's Sony Center with its distinctive roof, framed against the surrounding glass towers, especially striking after dark. The middle of the square lies to the south of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and tilt the phone upwards slightly, keeping the verticals straight by lining the towers up with the grid. Let the roof fill the top of the frame and leave some square or pavement at the bottom for scale. For a different view, the Panoramapunkt or the Reichstag are both alternatives. From the Reichstag you will need the telephoto lens to pick out the Sony Center.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: After dark, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body or lean on a solid surface to keep the image sharp. Tap on the brightest part of the roof to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the lights do not wash out.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: After dark, when the Sony Center roof and the towers around it are at their most striking. Daytime also works well for a clear view of the whole square.

text.access_note: The square itself is an open public space; for the Panoramapunkt or the Reichstag dome, check the official site before you go, as booking may be needed.
claims_not_in_sources: A phone's night mode usually copes better with lit buildings if you hold the phone steady against your body or a solid surface.
Tilting the phone upwards makes tall buildings lean inwards unless the verticals are lined up with the gridlines.
The square is open to walk around at any time, as it is a public space.

name: Berlin TV Tower
label: TV Tower
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Karl-Liebknecht-Straße' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Karl-Liebknecht-Straße nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/556435241: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Fernsehturm Berlin' (43 m across).
notes: 368 m tall landmark by Alexanderplatz.

text.description:
The Berlin TV Tower is the tall needle with a silver sphere that you can see from most of the city. East Germany's government built it between 1965 and 1969 as a broadcasting mast and a statement of power. At 368 metres including the antenna, it is the tallest structure in Germany. Today it is a symbol of the whole of Berlin, and it often appears as the opening shot in films set in the city.

This stand-here point gives the classic postcard view rather than a close-up of the tower. On Karl-Liebknecht-Straße, near the Marienkirche, the tower rises behind the cross and spire of the church, with traffic on the street in front. The church's old stonework and the tower's slim, modern shape make an unusual pairing, which is why guides and photo archives keep returning to this angle.

The sphere has a visitor platform about 203 metres up, and the tower is next to Alexanderplatz in the Marien Quarter. Everything else is easy to see from the street, so you only need to look up. Keep the tower upright in the frame and let the church cross sit close to it. Wait for a gap in the traffic if you want a cleaner foreground, and stay on the pavement.

If you have time for a second view, try Ebertsbrücke for the tower across the river with the Bode Museum, or Dircksenstrasse for the tower above the elevated railway tracks.
text.geographic_location: In the Marien Quarter of the Mitte district, in central Berlin. The tower stands just south-west of Alexanderplatz station, east of the Marienkirche (St Mary's Church).
text.directions_text: Start at Alexanderplatz, where U-Bahn and S-Bahn lines, trams and buses stop; the tower stands just south-west of the station. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole tower, the church spire and the street into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer picture. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the tower and the church cross closer together.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Karl-Liebknecht-Straße (stretch near the Marienkirche, looking east toward the tower). The tower rising behind the cross and spire of the Marienkirche, with traffic on the street in the foreground. The tower is to the south-east of you, and from here it rises behind the cross and spire of the church, with the street's traffic in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn your phone upright and switch on the gridlines. Place the church cross and spire on one side and the tower's shaft on the other, so the sphere sits in the upper part of the frame. Keep the horizon level so the tower does not lean. For a different view, try Ebertsbrücke (tower and Bode Museum across the river) or Dircksenstrasse (tower above the railway tracks).
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower's sphere to focus. Then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not wash out and the sphere keeps its detail. A Live Photo can catch passing traffic if you want some movement in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the sky has some colour or clouds, since a plain white sky makes the tower hard to pick out. Early in the day usually means fewer people on the pavement.

text.access_note: The viewpoint is on an open public street, but the Marienkirche is closed to visitors during services, and the tower's own visitor platform may be ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early in the day usually means fewer people on the pavement.
A plain white sky makes the tower harder to pick out than a sky with some colour or cloud.
Sliding the exposure down slightly can help keep detail in the sphere against a bright sky.
The street near the Marienkirche has regular traffic, so you should stay on the pavement.

name: Museum Island
label: Museum Island
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Lustgarten' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Lustgarten' (way/16000014): middle (272 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/330840129: large area 'Museum Island' (689 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: UNESCO ensemble of five museums on the Spree.

text.description: Museum Island is a cluster of grand museum buildings on the northern part of the Spree island, in the historic heart of Berlin. Most of it was built between 1830 and 1930, and it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1999. For a phone photo, the easiest and most rewarding frame is from the Lustgarten, the open lawn in front of the Altes Museum. From there the long colonnade of the Altes Museum and the dome of the Berliner Dom sit together, with the lawn and fountain filling the foreground. The Altes Museum is the oldest museum on the island and opened in 1830 to a design by Karl Friedrich Schinkel. The Bode Museum, on the island's northern tip, opened in 1904. Another good frame is the curved front of the Bode Museum across the water from the Monbijoubrücke. The Friedrichsbrücke gives you river lines and museum facades, with the cathedral in the distance. The Pergamon Museum is closed for major renovation, so its facade may be covered by scaffolding, and there are building works elsewhere on the island. Check how each spot looks before you go. Keep your phone level so the columns stay straight, and use the fountain or the lawn to give the frame some depth. Expect other visitors around the fountain and include them if you like, as they show the scale of the buildings.
text.geographic_location: Museum Island sits in Berlin's historic centre, on the northern part of the Spree island. The Lustgarten park and the Berliner Dom stand beside the museums.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Lustgarten in Berlin's historic centre. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the Altes Museum and the Berliner Dom together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole colonnade, the fountain and the dome in one frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the dome or the columns.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Lustgarten (on the south-west side of the Altes Museum, facing the Berliner Dom). The Berliner Dom and the colonnaded Altes Museum together, with the Lustgarten lawn and fountain in the foreground. Museum Island lies to the north-west of this point.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the colonnade up with a horizontal line so the building does not lean. Put the fountain or a strip of lawn in the lower third and the dome and museum front above it. If the fountain area is busy, step a little to one side and wait for a gap. For a different view, try the Bode Museum's curved front and dome from the Monbijoubrücke.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps some colour and the stonework is not washed out. Keep the lens clean, since you will be shooting outdoors in all weathers.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually means softer light and fewer people around the fountain. Midday sun can look flat and bright on the pale stonework.

text.access_note: The Lustgarten is a free open-air park. For the museums, check the official museum sites for entry details before you go.

name: Unter den Linden
label: Unter den Linden
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Pariser Platz' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Pariser Platz' (way/38210407): middle (193 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/9187708: large area 'Unter den Linden' (1276 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Grand tree-lined boulevard through historic Berlin.

text.description: Unter den Linden is the grand tree-lined boulevard that runs through the heart of Mitte, from the Berlin Palace in the east to the Brandenburg Gate in the west. It is named after the linden trees along its central walkway and two broad carriageways. It photographs well because everything lines up: two long rows of trees, wide pavements and the gate closing the view at one end. The easiest place to take the picture is Pariser Platz, at the gate end of the avenue. The linden trees you see today were replanted in the 1950s, after most of the earlier ones were lost in the 1930s and the last days of the war. Along the avenue you pass the Zeughaus (built 1695-1706, the oldest building on the street) and Schinkel's Neue Wache of 1817. Frederick the Great's equestrian statue has stood on the central strip since 1851. On Pariser Platz, step aside from the middle of the square, where most people shoot from, and use the trees or a streetlight as a natural frame. Try a few different angles, both from the square and along the boulevard. If you want a second viewpoint, the Schlossbrücke shows the avenue running away toward the gate, and the Marx-Engels-Brücke gives a view along the avenue with the Zeughaus beside it. The gate end is busy with visitors, so go early if you can.
text.geographic_location: Unter den Linden is in the central Mitte district of Berlin. It runs from the Berlin Palace and Museum Island to Pariser Platz and the Brandenburg Gate.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from central Mitte, near the Brandenburg Gate, or come by taxi or hired scooter and ask for Pariser Platz. Follow the line of the linden trees along the boulevard. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the gate and the trees together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the crowds or the width of the square stop you stepping back. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to squeeze the tree lines together along the avenue.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Pariser Platz (Stand a little back from the gate on the Unter den Linden side, not in the middle of the square). The Brandenburg Gate framed at the western end of the boulevard, with the avenue's tree lines leading toward the viewer. The part of the avenue marked on the map lies to the east, so turn that way for the long view down the trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the verticals of the gate straight. Use a tree trunk or streetlight at the edge of the frame so the picture feels framed rather than a snapshot from the crowd. Try the avenue's tree lines as leading lines, and look at the Schlossbrücke as an alternative view.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the gate to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little at sunset so the sky keeps its colour. Take a few shots at different zoom levels, as the crowds change what works.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or around sunset, before the tour groups arrive. The Christmas lights along the boulevard in winter are a seasonal option.

text.access_note: Check the official site for events or closures before you go.

name: Gendarmenmarkt
label: Gendarmenmarkt
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Konzerthaus Berlin' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Konzerthaus Berlin' (way/217512230): middle (100 m across); moved 25 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/844740667: 'Schiller Monument', the best-known feature inside 'Gendarmenmarkt' (344 m across).
notes: Baroque square with the Konzerthaus and two cathedrals.

text.description:
Gendarmenmarkt is a formal square in central Berlin with three grand buildings arranged around it: the Konzerthaus on one side, and the French and German Cathedrals facing each other across it. A statue of the poet Friedrich Schiller stands in the middle. The square dates from the end of the seventeenth century and was reconstructed in 1773. The French Cathedral was built by the Huguenot community between 1701 and 1705, and Karl Friedrich Schinkel designed the Konzerthaus in 1821. Most of the buildings were badly damaged or destroyed in the Second World War, and all have since been restored.

It photographs well because everything is balanced. The two domed towers mirror each other, and the concert hall's wide steps give you a natural centre line. The lion statue and steps fill the foreground, and the statue of Schiller sits a little to your right. The German Cathedral, the mirror-image tower, is to the south, behind you. For a different angle, you could try Markgrafenstraße for a view across the whole square, but this is an older recommendation, so check on site that it still works. The square also hosts a popular Christmas market, which can fill the space and the steps, so expect a different scene at that time of year.
text.geographic_location: Gendarmenmarkt is a square in the Friedrichstadt part of central Berlin (Mitte), framed by the Konzerthaus and the French and German Cathedrals.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Friedrichstadt area of central Berlin and ask your taxi or hired scooter to take you to Gendarmenmarkt. From there the Schiller statue is about 1 minute on foot to the north-east. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the steps, the lion statue and the French Cathedral's tower into one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a calmer view, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the dome and its details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Konzerthaus Berlin (central steps, facing north toward the Französischer Dom). The symmetrical square framed by the French Cathedral on one side and the German Cathedral on the other, with the concert hall's lion statue and steps in the foreground. The Schiller statue is a little to your right, towards the north-east. The German Cathedral, the mirror-image tower, is to the south, behind you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and put the French Cathedral on the centre line, with the lion statue and steps below it. Keep the phone level so the towers don't lean. For an alternative, you could try Markgrafenstraße for a wider view of the square, but this is an older recommendation, so check on site that the viewpoint still works.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the cathedral to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour. In the evening, night mode helps, but hold the phone steady against a railing or your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon or dusk usually gives softer light and lit-up buildings. Early in the day tends to be quieter on the steps.

text.access_note: The square and the steps are outside views in public space, but the French Cathedral's viewing platform is ticketed, and events such as the Christmas market can change access, so check the official site before you go.

name: Humboldt Forum
label: Humboldt Forum
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Lustgarten' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Lustgarten' (way/16000014): middle (272 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/8413352835: the OpenStreetMap point 'Humboldt Forum'.
notes: Rebuilt Berlin Palace with its baroque facades.

text.description: The Humboldt Forum is a museum of world cultures and art housed in the reconstructed Berlin Palace on Museum Island. It is named after the Prussian scholars Wilhelm and Alexander von Humboldt. It opened to the public on 20 July 2021, and its last wing followed in September 2022. That is why this spot works: the wide lawn and paving give you space to step back, so the long facade fits in one frame without craning your neck. Look for the Portal V passage and the replica of the Sanchi gate set into the facade, which add colour and detail to what is otherwise a formal stone front. The Altes Museum stands beside you, so a little of it can frame one edge of the picture. The view is at ground level and needs no ticket. If you want a second angle, the roof terrace looks back over the Lustgarten, Berlin Cathedral and Museum Island, and Schlossbrücke shows the west facade and dome over the water. Check the official site before you go to confirm that the terrace is open and what photography is allowed inside. Drones are not permitted over Museum Island.
text.geographic_location: The Humboldt Forum is on Museum Island in the historic centre of Berlin. The Lustgarten lies just to its north-west, beside the Altes Museum.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for Museum Island in central Berlin. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole north front and the open square. Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Switch to telephoto (2x-3x, depending on your phone) to pick out Portal V and the Sanchi gate replica.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Lustgarten (near the Altes Museum, facing the north facade). The north facade of the Humboldt Forum framing the Lustgarten, with the Portal V passage and the Sanchi gate replica on the facade.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the facade up with the horizontal lines so the walls look straight. Hold the phone level, since tilting it makes the building lean. Leave some lawn or sky in the frame to show the scale of the square. Try a tighter telephoto shot of the Sanchi gate replica as a second picture. For a different view, the Schlossbrücke shows the west facade and dome over the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. Take a few shots in case people walk through.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft, even daylight suits the stone front, and early morning is likely to be quieter in the square. Check the sky on the day, as an overcast sky gives flatter but even light.

text.access_note: The Lustgarten is an open public space, but the Humboldt Forum itself, its roof terrace and its exhibitions have their own entry and photography rules, so check the official site before you go.

name: Berlin Victory Column
label: Victory Column
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Straße des 17. Juni' (1 web pages); placed at the stretch of Straße des 17. Juni nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/718035022: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Victory Column' (84 m across).
notes: Golden Victoria on a column in the Tiergarten.

text.description:
The Victory Column (Siegessäule) is a tall stone monument topped by a gilded bronze figure of Victoria, the Roman goddess of victory. Berliners call her Goldelse, roughly "Golden Lizzy". It was designed by Heinrich Strack and opened on 2 September 1873 to mark Prussian victories. It first stood on Königsplatz (now Platz der Republik), then in 1938–39 was moved to the Großer Stern roundabout, where it stands now. At that point it was made taller, and it reaches about 67 metres today. It photographs well because it stands alone in the middle of the roundabout, with the gold figure standing out against the sky and trees.

Use gridlines to keep the column central, and leave a little sky above Victoria. Keep to the pavements: the column sits inside a busy roundabout. For a classic postcard alternative, try Straße des 17. Juni, the tree-lined avenue west of the roundabout, where the column rises over the junction with the Brandenburg Gate lined up behind it. For another, more unusual view, the Großer Stern has pedestrian tunnels. If the entrances are open, the stairs and walls make strong leading lines for a low shot looking up. The viewing platform needs a ticket, and your photos from up there will not include the column itself, so it is better to shoot from the ground.
text.geographic_location: The column stands in the middle of the Großer Stern roundabout in central Berlin. Straße des 17. Juni runs through it towards the Brandenburg Gate.
text.directions_text: No Underground, S-Bahn or tram stop is listed for this spot. Stay on the pavements around the Großer Stern roundabout. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from where you stand. If you try the avenue view along Straße des 17. Juni as an alternative, the telephoto (2x–5x, depending on your phone) can bring the Brandenburg Gate closer behind the column. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) only for the low shot from the tunnel stairs.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Straße des 17. Juni (avenue west of the Großer Stern roundabout, looking east toward the column). The column rising over the roundabout with the Brandenburg Gate behind it along the tree-lined avenue. Stay on the pavement and out of traffic.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the column on the central vertical line. Keep Victoria well clear of the top edge. For the avenue alternative, keep the avenue straight with its trees on both sides. As another alternative, from the Großer Stern tunnel stairs (if open) the whole column fits in an ultra-wide shot looking up, with the walls leading the eye.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the column to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the gold figure keeps its detail against the bright sky. Check that your lens is clean, because city traffic makes it smudgy.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Golden hour is the time recommended by a visitor guide, when the light is soft and the gold glows. Arriving early also helps to avoid crowds.

text.access_note: The column and the roundabout are open public space that you can photograph from the pavements and tunnels, but the viewing platform is ticketed, so check the official site before you go.

name: Bebelplatz
label: Bebelplatz
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Unter den Linden' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Unter den Linden nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/205728152: 'Memorial for the Nazi book burnings', the best-known feature inside 'Bebelplatz' (157 m across).
notes: Square with the State Opera and the Empty Library memorial.

text.description:
Bebelplatz is a broad, open square in the middle of Berlin, ringed by 18th-century buildings. The State Opera stands on one side, St. Hedwig's Cathedral with its copper dome sits at the south-east corner, and the Old Library and the Humboldt University buildings close in the rest. The square was laid out between 1741 and 1743 under Frederick II of Prussia, and the buildings were restored in the 1950s after wartime damage. It photographs well because everything fits into one calm, symmetrical view, with plenty of sky and pale stone.

It is also the place where, on 10 May 1933, around 20,000 books were burned in a Nazi ceremony. Micha Ullman's memorial, the Empty Library, marks the spot. A glass panel set into the cobbles lets you look down into a room of bare white bookshelves, big enough to hold every one of those books. A line from Heinrich Heine is set into the ground nearby too.

For the classic overview, stand on the pavement of Unter den Linden and look south across the square. Take one wide shot there, then walk in to photograph the glass panel looking straight down. The cathedral's dome and columned front make a good third picture, but the cathedral has been under renovation, so check whether the exterior is accessible before you plan a shot around it.
text.geographic_location: Bebelplatz is in the central Mitte district of Berlin, on the south side of the Unter den Linden boulevard. It surrounds the State Opera and sits next to Humboldt University and St. Hedwig's Cathedral.
text.directions_text: There is no station close by, so head for Unter den Linden in central Mitte, by taxi or hired scooter, and ask for Bebelplatz. The square lies directly south of you, across the road. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole square in. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the cathedral's dome and the opera facade.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Unter den Linden (the sidewalk on the north side of the boulevard, looking south across the square). The whole square, with the State Opera on the left, St. Hedwig's Cathedral centre-left, and the Old Library and Humboldt law school on the right. Pick a point where the square opens up in front of you. For the memorial, walk onto the square and stand over the glass panel.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the buildings upright by lining the vertical edges up with the grid. Leave the open cobbled space in the foreground to give a sense of scale. At the glass panel, point the phone straight down and let the white shelves fill the frame. As an alternative view, shoot the cathedral's dome and columned front framed against the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the glass panel to focus on the shelves below, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if reflections wash out the picture. Shade the screen with your body or hand to cut glare. Turn off Live Photos if you don't want movement from passers-by.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go early in the day if you want the square with fewer people in it. Soft daylight suits the pale stone best.

text.access_note: Bebelplatz is an open public square, but the cathedral and opera house are separate buildings, so check the official sites before you go if you want to go inside or onto the cathedral steps.

name: Oberbaum Bridge
label: Oberbaum Bridge
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Mühlenstraße' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Mühlenstraße nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/288514442: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Oberbaumbrücke' (179 m across).
notes: Double-deck brick bridge over the Spree.

text.description:
The Oberbaum Bridge is a double-deck red-brick bridge over the River Spree, linking Friedrichshain and Kreuzberg. It was finished in 1896 and designed by Otto Stahn in the North German Brick Gothic style, like a small city gate, with pointed arches, coats of arms and two pointed towers. The towers were modelled on a gate tower in Prenzlau and are decorative rather than useful. Berlin U-Bahn lines U1 and U3 run along the upper deck, and the lower deck carries the road.

The bridge was badly damaged at the end of the Second World War and later sat on the Berlin Wall border. After reunification it was rebuilt, with a modern steel middle section by Santiago Calatrava. It reopened on 9 November 1994.

It photographs well because the brick, the towers and the water make a tidy composition, and a train crossing the upper deck adds movement. The bridge is to the south-west, with the Spree in front of it. This is the classic angle, and it works well when the sun is low behind the bridge. It is also right beside the East Side Gallery, so you can combine both in one walk. For a different view, Elsenbrücke shows the bridge with the TV Tower behind it.
text.geographic_location: The bridge crosses the River Spree in Berlin, between Friedrichshain on the north bank and Kreuzberg on the south bank. The Friedrichshain viewpoint is next to the East Side Gallery.
text.directions_text: Head for the Friedrichshain riverbank beside the East Side Gallery. Look for the small outcrop on Mühlenstraße between the Wall Museum and the bridge. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the bridge, both towers and the river sit naturally in the frame. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more water and sky in the foreground. Try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the towers and arches.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Mühlenstraße (Friedrichshain riverbank, small outcrop between the bridge and the Wall Museum, beside the East Side Gallery). The red-brick Oberbaum Bridge with its towers in front of a sunset sky, with the Spree in the foreground. Stay on the bank and well away from the roadway and the tracks.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the bridge on the lower third, with the water below and plenty of sky above. Keep the horizon level and the towers upright. Wait for a U-Bahn train to cross the upper deck and take a few shots, or use Live Photos to catch the movement. For a different angle, Elsenbrücke shows the bridge with the TV Tower and city centre behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bridge to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the brick does not turn into a silhouette. After sunset, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body to keep the shot sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon to early evening, in the golden hour before sunset, or the blue hour just after.

text.access_note: The bridge and the riverbank viewpoint are open public spaces, but the bridge carries road traffic, cyclists and trains, so keep clear of the roadway and tracks.
claims_not_in_sources: The sun sets in the west, and the angle works best when the sun is low in the south-west to west, such as in autumn and winter.
Lowering the exposure slider helps keep the sky's colour when shooting toward a bright sunset sky.
Night mode works better if you brace your elbows against your body to keep the phone steady.

name: Rotes Rathaus
label: Red City Hall
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Neptunbrunnen' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Neptunbrunnen' (way/23813204): middle (21 m across); moved 10 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/4211905: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Red City Hall' (185 m across).
notes: Red-brick city hall with a terracotta frieze.

text.description:
The Rotes Rathaus, or Red Town Hall, is Berlin's city hall, and it is easy to spot from a distance: a long red-brick building with a tall clock tower in the middle. It was designed by Hermann Friedrich Waesemann in the Renaissance Revival style and finished in 1869. The main front is 25 bays wide, with a five-stage tower at the centre. The tower was originally 94 metres high and the clock sits on its top stage. The building was badly damaged in the Second World War and rebuilt to the original plans in the early 1950s. It reopened on 30 November 1955 and became the town hall for East Berlin. Since 1991 it has housed the Governing Mayor of Berlin and the Senate, and the clock was re-gilded in 2006.

It photographs well because the warm red brick stands out against the sky and the tower gives a clear centre line. The best-known shot is from the Neptunbrunnen, where the bronze Neptune Fountain sits in the foreground and the facade and clock tower rise behind it. For a different angle, try Spandauer Straße for a side-on view of the brickwork, or Alexanderplatz for the town hall as a backdrop to the square. Each of those two rests on a single recommendation, so judge them when you arrive. Roadworks in front of the building can block the fountain angles, so check what is there on the day. This is a busy area and pickpockets are reported, so keep your phone strap and bag secure while you frame the shot.
text.geographic_location: The Rotes Rathaus stands on Rathausstraße in central Berlin, a short walk from Alexanderplatz.
text.directions_text: Head for Alexanderplatz, as the town hall is on Rathausstraße close beside it. The Neptunbrunnen in front of the building is the recommended viewpoint for the classic shot, and it is a short walk from there. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the fountain, the full width of the facade and the tower in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched look. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the clock and tower details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (in front of the building, framing the fountain against the facade). The red-brick Neo-Renaissance facade and clock tower rising behind the bronze Neptune Fountain in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and put the tower on the central vertical line, with the fountain low in the foreground. Keep your phone level so the tall tower doesn't lean. If the fountain angles are blocked by works, try Spandauer Straße for a side-on view of the facade instead.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brick wall to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour and the red brick stays rich. If you shoot at dusk, use night mode and hold your phone steady against your body or a solid ledge.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the day is usually calmer, with fewer people crossing your frame. Check for roadworks before you go, whatever the hour.

text.access_note: The town hall is a working government building, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside. Roadworks may affect the square in front of the building.
claims_not_in_sources: Early in the day is usually calmer with fewer people.
Night mode works best if the phone is held steady against a solid surface.

name: Neue Wache
label: Neue Wache
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Unter den Linden' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Unter den Linden nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/24240381: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'New Guard House' (41 m across).
notes: Neoclassical memorial building by Schinkel.

text.description: The Neue Wache ("New Watchhouse") is a calm, flat-fronted neoclassical building on Unter den Linden, in the historic centre of Berlin. Karl Friedrich Schinkel designed it, and it was built between 1816 and 1818 as a guardhouse for the Royal Palace and a memorial to the Liberation Wars. It is regarded as a major work of Prussian Neoclassical architecture. For a phone photo, the appeal is its clean geometry: a portico of plain Doric columns, a sculpted frieze above, and sturdy corner blocks on either side. The building sits a little back from the avenue, so you can fit the whole front in one frame without tilting the phone much. Its purpose has changed several times. Since 1993 it has been the Central Memorial of the Federal Republic of Germany to the Victims of War and Tyranny. Inside, an enlarged version of Käthe Kollwitz's sculpture Mother with her Dead Son stands directly beneath an open circular skylight, so it is exposed to the weather. From the street, keep the whole facade in view and use the columns for rhythm. If you want a second angle, Bebelplatz gives a view across an open square, with the portico framed by the buildings around it. If you go inside, guides advise against using flash near the central sculpture, and it is a memorial, so be quiet and respectful.
text.geographic_location: In the Mitte district, on the Unter den Linden boulevard in the historic centre of Berlin, between the Zeughaus and Humboldt University.
text.directions_text: Head for the Unter den Linden boulevard in the historic centre of Berlin, close to the Zeughaus and Humboldt University. The area is best reached on foot along the boulevard. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the whole facade with its portico and frieze. If people or traffic force you in close, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x), but keep the phone level so the columns don't lean. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the frieze, the pediment sculpture or the column tops.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Unter den Linden (north side of the boulevard, opposite the Zeughaus). The full neoclassical street facade with its Doric portico and frieze, set a few metres back from the avenue. This is the classic postcard angle.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the central columns up with the middle of the frame, so the symmetry looks deliberate. Keep the phone upright and level to avoid slanting verticals. Leave a little pavement or sky around the building rather than cropping tight. For a different view, try Bebelplatz, where the building is seen across the open square.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stone facade to set focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly if the sky is bright, so the pale stone keeps its detail. If you go inside, turn the flash off and tap on the sculpture, then adjust the exposure slider so the bright opening above doesn't wash it out.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daylight shows the stone and the frieze best, and early in the day is usually quieter on the pavement. Dusk is also worth trying with night mode, held steady against a lamp post or railing.

text.access_note: The outside can be photographed from the public boulevard; the interior is a memorial hall, so check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements and any closures.

name: Kaiser Wilhelm Memorial Church
label: Memorial Church
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Breitscheidplatz' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Breitscheidplatz' (way/491328295): middle (339 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/15218371: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'New Kaiser Wilhelm Memorial Church' (52 m across).
notes: Ruined church left as a war memorial.

text.description: The Kaiser Wilhelm Memorial Church is a famous landmark of western Berlin, and what makes it so photogenic is the contrast. The broken spire of the old church, built in the 1890s and badly damaged in an air raid in 1943, was kept as a ruin. Around it stand the modern buildings put up between 1959 and 1963, designed by Egon Eiermann. The new church walls are a concrete honeycomb holding 21,292 pieces of stained glass, mostly blue, so the ruined tower and the glowing glass sit side by side. Berliners nickname the old tower "the hollow tooth", and the spire now stands about 71 metres high. Start wide, then step in for a closer shot of the blue glass or the texture of the ruined stonework. Keep the phone level so the vertical lines stay straight. The square can fill with market stalls, performers and crowds, so look for a gap, or wait a moment for people to move. If you go inside, avoid flash and be considerate of anyone there to pray.
text.geographic_location: The church stands in the middle of Breitscheidplatz, right beside the Kurfürstendamm shopping boulevard, in the western part of central Berlin.
text.directions_text: Head for Breitscheidplatz at the Kurfürstendamm end in western Berlin; by taxi or hired scooter, ask for the Memorial Church (Gedächtniskirche). From there the church is about 1 minute on foot, to the west. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) so the old tower and the new blue-glass church fit together with the square. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view, and to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the top of the ruined spire.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Breitscheidplatz (from across the plaza). The broken old tower and the modern blue-glass church together in one frame, with the surrounding plaza.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and keep the tower upright against a vertical line. Leave some of the plaza in the bottom of the frame to show the scale. For a different view, try the church from the Kurfürstendamm, with the ruined tower as the focal point.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky and the blue glass keep their colour. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone steady against your body or a solid surface. Inside, turn the flash off.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime is good for the blue glass and clear views of the ruin. In the evening the floodlit tower is a good subject from the square, so try night mode then.

text.access_note: The square is open public space, but the church is a place of worship and the ruined tower may have limited access, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Breitscheidplatz can be busy with market stalls, performers and demonstrations, which can get in the way of clean shots.
The stained glass shows its colour best in daylight.
Lowering the exposure slider helps keep sky and glass colour in the frame.
